title: Americans Now View Ultra-Processed Foods as Addictive as Alcohol — and a Bipartisan Majority Wants the Government to Act
excerpt: A landmark Cornell survey of 2,000 adults finds rare bipartisan consensus: over 60% see UPFs as a major cause of obesity, diabetes, and heart disease, with parallels to tobacco drawing calls for regulation that could reshape what NRI families eat in America.
body:
More than 60 percent of Americans now believe ultra-processed foods are addictive — and a growing body of research suggests they may be right. A first-of-its-kind national survey, published this month in the *American Journal of Public Health* by researchers at Cornell University, has found a rare consensus across political lines: a bipartisan majority of U.S. adults sees ultra-processed foods as a major driver of obesity, Type 2 diabetes, and heart disease, and wants the government to step in.

The findings arrive at a pivotal moment for food policy in the United States, with researchers drawing explicit parallels to the public awakening that eventually led to tobacco regulation — a comparison that should concern every immigrant family navigating the American grocery aisle.

## What the Cornell Study Found

The researchers surveyed a nationally representative sample of 2,000 U.S. adults and discovered a striking level of agreement. More than 60 percent of respondents identified ultra-processed foods — think packaged snacks, sugary cereals, instant noodles, frozen meals, and soft drinks — as addictive and as major causes of chronic disease.

Participants rated the health risks of ultra-processed foods as roughly equivalent to alcohol and significantly worse than fast food or cannabis. More than 80 percent supported requiring the government to test lab-made food chemicals for safety before they reach shelves. About two-thirds backed national education campaigns, restrictions on advertising to children, banning artificial dyes, and adding warning labels to packaging.

"Ultraprocessed foods have entered public consciousness as a major health hazard," said Jeff Niederdeppe, a professor of communication at Cornell and the study's lead author. "The convergence of public belief, bipartisan support, and scientific evidence creates a critical window for policy action."

## The Tobacco Playbook



> **""Ultraprocessed foods have entered public consciousness as a major health hazard," said Jeff Niederdeppe, a professor of communication at Cornell and the study's lead author."**


What makes the Cornell findings particularly striking is the political dimension. In earlier debates over soda taxes and obesity policy, conservatives typically pushed back, citing personal freedom. This time, a majority across party lines agreed that corporate strategies — not individual willpower — shape dietary choices.

A separate review published in the *Milbank Quarterly* makes the tobacco comparison explicit. Researchers found that ultra-processed foods share five key engineering strategies with industrially produced cigarettes: dose optimization, delivery speed, hedonic (pleasure) engineering, environmental ubiquity, and deceptive reformulation — think "light" cigarettes rebranded as "low-fat" snacks.

"A similar shift in narrative seems poised to accelerate momentum for reform around ultra-processed foods," the Cornell researchers wrote. "The American public is not a barrier to progress — it may be the catalyst."

## The Scale of the Problem

Ultra-processed foods now make up roughly 58 percent of total calories consumed by American adults and nearly 67 percent for children and adolescents, according to NHANES data. A growing stack of observational evidence — including a 2024 Lancet study of over 266,000 Europeans — links higher UPF intake to a 9 percent increased risk of developing multiple chronic diseases simultaneously: cancer, cardiovascular disease, and Type 2 diabetes.

A Tufts University study published in the *American Journal of Public Health* went further, finding that the processing itself — not just the nutritional profile — independently worsens health outcomes. Changes to food structure, loss of beneficial compounds, additives, and packaging chemicals all appear to play a role.

## Why This Matters for the Diaspora

For South Asian families in the United States, the ultra-processed food conversation is not abstract. The transition from a traditional Indian diet — rich in lentils, whole grains, fresh vegetables, and home-cooked meals — to the convenience-driven American food landscape has been well documented in nutrition research.

South Asians already face a significantly higher baseline risk of Type 2 diabetes and cardiovascular disease compared to the general U.S. population. The MASALA study, based at Northwestern University, has shown that South Asian Americans develop metabolic risk factors like insulin resistance and prediabetes at younger ages and lower body weights than other ethnic groups.

Adding ultra-processed foods on top of this genetic predisposition creates what researchers call a "double burden" — the metabolic vulnerability of the community meets the engineered overconsumption of the American food system.

The policy actions Americans now support — chemical testing, warning labels, advertising restrictions on children — could directly reshape what lands in NRI shopping carts and school lunchboxes across the country.

## What Comes Next

Policy experts say the window is narrow but real. The bipartisan consensus revealed by the Cornell survey is unusual in today's polarized political climate and mirrors the kind of public opinion shift that preceded the Master Settlement Agreement with tobacco companies in the late 1990s.

Whether that translates into actual legislation — front-of-pack warning labels, restrictions on food marketing to children, or additive testing requirements — remains to be seen. But the direction is clear: Americans have moved from debating whether ultra-processed foods are harmful to asking what the government should do about it.

For diaspora families already juggling the demands of preserving traditional food culture while adapting to American convenience, the message is reinforced by both the science and the sentiment: the thali may be the best defence against a food system that is, increasingly, designed to work against you.

*Sources: American Journal of Public Health (June 2026), Cornell University, Milbank Quarterly, Tufts University, The Lancet Regional Health — Europe*
